title: Faith the best wealth
hook: a fierce spirit orders the Buddha in and out, then threatens him with a riddle

segments.voice: Yesterday: two mountain spirits checking references, and your line, they spoke well of him. Did you say your good word? Today, a much less friendly spirit. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Get out. So the Buddha gets up and goes out. Come in. So he comes back in. Get out. He goes. Come in. He comes. The spirit is a yakkha named Alavaka, and this is his house, and he's testing how far he can push this calm visitor. The fourth time he says get out, the Buddha says: no, friend, I won't. Do what you have to do. And Alavaka makes his threat. I'll ask you a question. If you can't answer it, I'll scramble your mind, or split your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you across the Ganges. Today: faith the best wealth.
screen: `GET OUT. COME IN.` → `THE FOURTH TIME: NO.` → `ANSWER, OR ELSE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's reply is calm. In all the world, he says, I see no one who could scramble my mind or split my heart. But ask whatever you like. Notice the order of what he did. Three times, he went along. Not because he was afraid, the commentary says, but to soften a hard mind with gentleness. Only the fourth time, when obeying would have been just a game, did he say no. Then the questions come, in verse. What is the best wealth a person has? Faith, the Buddha answers, saddha, trust in what is good. What, practiced well, brings happiness? The teaching. What is the sweetest of all tastes? Truth. Living how is the best life? Living with wisdom. Then the deeper ones. How does one cross the flood? By faith. How does one cross the sea? By care, by not being careless. How does one get past suffering? By effort. How does one become pure? By wisdom. Why faith? One way to hear it: look at what the threat was. Alavaka could take everything: your mind, your body, your life. But trust in something good is a kind of wealth that's still yours while you're being threatened. It's what lets you answer calmly. And at the end, the fierce spirit says, in words close to yesterday's spirits, that he'll travel from village to village, honoring the one who is fully awake. Theravada chants still recall the taming of Alavaka.
screen: `THREE TIMES YES, THE FOURTH TIME NO` · `NO ONE CAN SPLIT MY HEART` · `THE BEST WEALTH IS FAITH` · `CROSS THE FLOOD BY TRUST` · then, large: `FAITH THE BEST WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse one calm answer. Sit and settle. Think of a small threat you face: a demanding message, a tense meeting, a sharp relative. Picture it arriving. Notice any jolt in the chest. Now breathe out slowly, and picture yourself answering the way the Buddha did: not shrinking, not striking back. Just steady. Ask what it is they want, and answer plainly. Let your shoulders drop. Notice what's still yours. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
saddha. The Buddha's first answer to the threatening spirit Alavaka: trust in what is good is a person's best wealth. Today's word.
Your line: answer once, calmly and plainly. When something pushes you today, answer once from that steady place, calmly and plainly. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 587 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY AS IT IS.`

howItsDone: The taming of Alavaka is one of the episodes recalled in the Jayamangala Gatha, a verse chant of the Buddha's victories recited in Theravada temples and homes.

myth: the Buddha refuses Alavaka's very first order
he goes out and comes in three times, and only refuses the fourth.
Alavaka threatens to throw him across the Ganges
if he can't answer the riddles: or scramble his mind, or split his heart.
the Buddha says truth is the sweetest of tastes
and faith is a person's best wealth.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. for the fourth time, the spirit orders you out of his house. what do you do?
options: leave again, to keep the peace.
say no, calmly: do what you must.
fork.reveal: he went along three times to soften a hard mind; the fourth time he declined calmly, and the questions began.

original.note: Pali Alavaka: the spirit of Alavi, named for the town where the story is set.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith as the best wealth means believing is better than having money.
what it means: one way to hear it, trust in what is good is wealth a threat can't take, and it lets you answer calmly.
what a scholar hears: the Alavaka Sutta (Sn 1.10, also SN 10.12) pairs faith with crossing the flood; later tradition makes the taming of Alavaka one of the eight victories of the Jayamangala chant.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.10, Alavaka Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 10.12)
Commentary on Sn 1.10: why the Buddha complied three times

notes: Sn 1.10 paraphrased. Confirm the out-and-in sequence (three times complied, refused the fourth), the threat (derange mind, split heart, throw across the Ganges), and the question-answer pairs: best wealth faith; well practiced dhamma brings happiness; truth sweetest of tastes; living by wisdom the best life; crossing the flood by faith, the sea by heedfulness, suffering by energy, purified by wisdom.
The commentary's reason for complying (to soften his mind) is given as the commentary's view.
Jayamangala Gatha mention in howItsDone: confirm Alavaka is among its eight episodes.
Pali name spelling with the retroflex l (Alavaka / Alavi); confirm Devanagari आळवक.

Editor review: the closing village-to-village vow now acknowledged as echoing yesterday's spirits (Sn 180 / Sn 192); narrator's interpretation of faith marked 'one way to hear it'; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; 'many temples' softened.
